newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Georgia, separatists closer to deal - negotiator.
newsitem.headline: Georgia, separatists closer to deal - negotiator.

text.p: Georgia and its breakaway region of Abkhazia have made progress towards a peace deal after several days of intense negotiations, a Russian official said on Thursday.

"This is a complicated problem, but progress has been achieved. It consists of the fact that today there is a better understanding on the Georgian and Abkhaz sides as to the essence of the problem," Boris Berezovsky, deputy secretary of the Kremlin's powerful Security Council, told reporters in Tbilisi.
Berezovsky carried out three days of shuttle diplomacy in which he met Georgian leader Eduard Shevardnadze three times and made two trips to Abkhazia for talks with separatist leaders.
He said the negotiations would continue, though he did not specify when or where.
Berezovsky said the thorniest issue was the return to Abkhazia of at least 150,000 ethnic Georgian refugees who fled the separatist military victory over Georgian troops in 1993.

"The Georgian and Abkhaz sides understand that there should be a guarantee of the refugees' safe return. The timetable for the return is the most complicated question. It will be the subject of future negotiations," he said.
Shevardnadze, speaking alongside Berezovsky, thanked him for his mediation efforts but declined to reveal specific details about the talks.
"The main thing is that now we have more optimism for the resolution of all the problems," he said.
A July 31 deadline has been set for the end of Russia's mandate in Abkhazia.

Georgia says the 1,500 troops patrolling a region along the de facto border between Georgia and Abkhazia must begin to leave after that date unless they agree to increase their functions, including helping the refugees to return and policing more of Abkhazia.
Russia has said that Abkhaz officials must also approve the new mandate, but they have so far opposed it.
Tbilisi has hinted that the issue of three former Soviet bases on its territory might also be raised if the Russian peacekeeping troops leave.
In March 1995, Georgia signed an agreement with Russia, which inherited the bases, allowing them to stay for 25 years, but neither side has ratified the deal.

Georgian military officials say the bases contain at least 20,000 troops. Russia refuses to give details about the bases, which have huge strategic importance as Moscow's only military bases outside Russia, apart from in nearby Armenia.

Abkhaz leader Vladislav Ardzinba was optimistic after meeting Berezovsky and the speaker of the Georgian parliament, Zurab Zhvaniya, for six hours in the separatist-held town of Novy Afon late on Tuesday.
"I think I am sufficiently optimistic to say that sooner or later we will find a solution to the problem. I think we are very close to that," he said.

His foreign minister, Sergei Shamba, was equally positive. "The fruit has ripened. New compromises have appeared on both sides and both sides understand that we have to resolve the problem without the application of force," he said.
Abkhazia, which had hoped that the international community would recognise its de facto independence at the end of the war, is now feeling the effects of three years of deep isolation.

No foreign state has forged ties with it and a partial blockade imposed by the Commonwealth of Independent States has ruined the tourism-driven economy of the lush, beautiful Black Sea subtropical region.
